summary: Defines the /.well-known/ path prefix, a reserved place on a site where standard files and metadata can be found at predictable locations. It also set up a registry for names under that prefix. It is no longer current, because it was replaced by RFC 8615.

eli5.summary: Every house keeps its fire plan in the same spot by the front door, so anyone who needs it knows exactly where to look.

questions: where to put site metadata files
how to register a well-known uri
subtitle: One reserved path prefix, /.well-known/, so sites can publish site-wide metadata without name collisions.

tldr.problem: More and more Web protocols need to find site-wide policy or metadata before making a request, and ad hoc fixed locations risk colliding with each other and with existing resources.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC reserves the path prefix /.well-known/ in HTTP and HTTPS URIs, and creates an IANA registry where each new name under that prefix must be registered.
tldr.outcome: Applications get predictable, collision-free locations for site-wide metadata. RFC 5785 was obsoleted by RFC 8615.

today: RFC 5785 was obsoleted by RFC 8615, which now defines well-known URIs. It had updated RFC 2616 and RFC 2818.

sections.title: The Problem with Ad Hoc Locations
sections.content:
Web-based protocols often need to discover policy or other information about a host, called site-wide metadata, before making a request. The RFC gives the Robots Exclusion Protocol and the Platform for Privacy Preferences as examples. Per-resource mechanisms such as HTTP headers or WebDAV's PROPFIND exist, but their perceived overhead in latency or deployment difficulty often rules them out.

So it is common to pick a fixed, "well-known location" for the data. That has a drawback: collisions with other such locations and with resources that already exist on the site. This memo addresses it by defining one path prefix, /.well-known/, for these locations.
sections.eli5: If every program picks its own secret spot on a website, two programs may pick the same one. One agreed spot, with a list, avoids the mix-ups.

sections.title: What a Well-Known URI Is
sections.content:
A well-known URI is a URI whose path begins with /.well-known/ and whose scheme is HTTP, HTTPS, or another scheme that has explicitly been specified to use well-known URIs. Applications that want a new well-known URI must register it. If an application registers the name example, the URI on http://www.example.com/ is http://www.example.com/.well-known/example. Registered names must conform to the segment-nz production in RFC 3986.

The RFC leaves a lot to each application. It defines neither how to determine the authority to use nor the scope of the metadata, and no format or media type exists for /.well-known/ itself; clients should not expect a resource there. A registration typically references a specification of the format and media type, and may add details such as extra path components, query strings or HTTP method handling.

The intended use is narrow. Well-known URIs are not for general information retrieval or for building large URI namespaces. They suit cases such as policy that must be evaluated before accessing a resource, or where several round trips would hurt performance.
sections.eli5: Websites keep their special notes in a folder with a fixed name. The folder itself is not a note, and only things on the official list may go in it.

sections.title: The Well-Known URI Registry
sections.content:
The memo establishes the well-known URI registry. Names are registered on the advice of one or more Designated Experts appointed by the IESG, under Specification Required. Experts may approve before the specification is published once they are satisfied that it will be.

Requests go to a review mailing list. Within 14 days the experts approve or deny, and denials should explain why and suggest fixes. Requests undetermined for longer than 21 days can be brought to the IESG's attention.

The registration template has four parts: the URI suffix (relative to /.well-known/), the change controller, the specification documents, and optional related information. For Standards Track RFCs the change controller is IETF.
sections.eli5: To put something in the special folder, you fill in a short form. A few experts look at it and usually answer within two weeks.

sections.title: Security Considerations and FAQ
sections.content:
The memo does not say how far metadata from a well-known URI applies, nor how to discover a well-known URI for an application; each application must define both. Those minting new URIs and the administrators deploying them should consider exposure of sensitive data, denial-of-service attacks, server and client authentication, DNS rebinding, and attacks where limited access to a server lets someone affect how well-known URIs are served.

The appendix FAQ admits that well-known locations are bad for the Web, but says they are commonly used for technical and social reasons, so the memo defines a "sandbox" for them. The name /.well-known was chosen because it is short, descriptive and not widely used. Per-directory locations such as /images/.well-known/ were rejected because they would raise collision risks and are too "chatty". Existing mechanisms such as P3P and robots.txt are unaffected until they choose to use it.
sections.eli5: The special folder is a convenience, not a safe. Each program that uses it has to think about who could read or tamper with what is inside.
